periods.brief: In the 1960s, I transformed comics by giving our heroes human flaws and personal struggles, turning Marvel into a legacy of risk and conviction.
periods.full:
In the 1960s, I remade ourselves as Marvel, starting with the Fantastic Four in 1961. They argued, had money problems, and Ben Grimm loathed his own form — Jack Kirby's art gave that raw energy. We were a gamble born from necessity, since Atlas was nearly gone.

Readers connected with the honesty, and the Marvel Age began.

Then came Spider-Man in 1962, with Steve Ditko. Peter Parker was a teenager burdened by guilt and responsibility, and the saying "with great power there must also come great responsibility" became our guiding thread.

In 1963 we debuted the X-Men, whose mutants were hated simply for being different, and the Avengers too. Both struggled initially, but we had faith. And in 1966, we introduced T'Challa, the Black Panther, without making a fuss — he was simply a great character.

Looking back, these risks and our stubborn belief made all the difference.

periods.label: 1970s

levels.sentence: In Amazing Spider-Man #121, I helped kill Gwen Stacy, Peter Parker's first love, and her death taught everyone that our stories could have real consequences, changing comics forever.
levels.paragraph: In Amazing Spider-Man #121, I was part of the team that killed Gwen Stacy, one of our most prominent supporting characters. The Green Goblin hurled her from the Brooklyn Bridge, and I felt the shockwave ripple across the industry. That issue taught me that our stories could have real consequences. Comics would never be the same.
levels.summary:
I was involved in writing the issue where Gwen Stacy, Peter Parker's first love, was killed. The Green Goblin threw her from the Brooklyn Bridge, and readers everywhere felt the shockwave.

It was a bold move that showed us all that even beloved characters could face permanent consequences.

The death of Gwen Stacy changed the comic book industry forever.

It made our stories feel more real and more impactful, and it set a new standard for what could happen in superhero comics. I'll never forget the controversy and the emotion that surrounded this decision.

periods.label: 1980s

levels.sentence: In the 1980s, my team and I told Jean Grey's tragic fall and redemption in the Dark Phoenix Saga, then created Secret Wars, unknowingly setting the template for every summer crossover to come.
levels.paragraph: In 1980, we told the Dark Phoenix Saga, watching Jean Grey be seduced by absolute power and choose sacrifice to save the universe; the tragedy still haunts me. In 1984 came the sheer excitement of Secret Wars, with every hero and villain on Battleworld. We gave Marvel Spider-Man's black costume and the Beyonder, and we had no idea we were inventing the modern event comic. Looking back, those two moments define the decade for me.
levels.summary:
In 1980, my team and I took Jean Grey from mortal mutant to cosmic Phoenix, then watched her corruption into the Dark Phoenix. We showed her seduction by absolute power and the terrible consequences, and her final act was one of sacrifice, destroying herself to save the universe.

The themes of power, identity, and redemption carried real emotional weight, and the story became legendary.

In 1984, the excitement of Secret Wars swept us up. We placed nearly every hero and villain on Battleworld and watched alliances form and break, and the unprecedented scale felt like something special.

We gave Spider-Man his symbiotic black costume and introduced the Beyonder as a cosmic mystery, unaware that we were creating the template for every summer event to follow. Looking back, that marketing bonanza and creative high shaped the future of Marvel.

levels.sentence: In 1996 we filed for Chapter 11, sold off characters, canceled books, and by 1998 we were breathing again, never forgetting the close call.
levels.paragraph: In 1996, we filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy, a humbling experience for a company built on heroes. We sold off characters and canceled books to survive. But we found a path back with better stories and a bullpen that remembered why we started. By 1998, we were breathing again, though we never forgot that close call.

periods.label: 2000s

levels.sentence: From the triumph of X-Men to the fracture of Civil War and the gamble of Iron Man, I witnessed Marvel rise, split, and reinvent itself into a cinematic powerhouse.
levels.paragraph: In 2000, X-Men gave us hope after bankruptcy, showing our characters as heroes on the big screen. Six years later, Civil War tore the Marvel Universe apart, forcing me to question who to trust. Then in 2008, Iron Man's success launched a shared cinematic universe that made us pioneers. Through every victory and scar, I felt the weight of our stories and the promise of what we could become.
levels.summary:
In 2000, I watched our children take the screen in X-Men, the first live-action portrayal of mutants. It was a lifeline for our company emerging from bankruptcy, and that premiere night filled me with pride and hope I hadn't felt in years.

In 2006, Civil War split the Marvel Universe down the middle. The Registration Act forced every super-powered being to choose a side, and I watched Captain America and Iron Man lead rival factions into devastating conflict.

Cap surrendered to end the bloodshed, only to be assassinated on the courthouse steps—lines between hero and villain dissolved, and I no longer knew who to trust.

In 2008, Iron Man opened, and I was a bundle of nerves and hope. Robert Downey Jr. played a flawed genius, and our gamble on a lesser-known hero redefined us forever.

With one ambitious post-credits scene at a time, we built a shared cinematic universe, and by the time The Avengers arrived in 2012, we had created something previously impossible. Watching our stories connect across films made me feel like a pioneer.

periods.label: 2010s

levels.sentence: From the first team-up to the final battle, the Avengers saga taught me that long-term storytelling can deliver heartbreak, triumph, and a goodbye worth savoring.
levels.paragraph: I first saw The Avengers in 2012, and it was the payoff to years of post-credits promises. Thanos shattered that happy feeling in 2018, and I watched half the universe vanish. A year later, Endgame brought them back, but only through the sacrifice of Iron Man. The final goodbye to him and Captain America left me with a bittersweet sense of closure for an epic saga.
levels.summary:
The journey began in 2012 with The Avengers, the first team-up. I loved the humor—Hulk smashing Loki was perfect comic relief—and the way it honored every promise from the earlier films. That kind of long-term storytelling, where a setup actually pays off, left me completely satisfied.

In 2018, the threat became real. Thanos won, and I watched half of Earth's heroes dissolve into dust. The 2019 finale of Endgame brought them back, but at a cost: Tony Stark's sacrifice and Steve Rogers' farewell. I said goodbye feeling both proud and heartbroken.

Reflecting on the Infinity Saga, I see it as a masterwork. It took us from a cave with scraps to a funeral in a garden, a perfect emotional arc. Even though it's hard to let go, I now feel closure and am ready to move forward.

periods.label: A life

levels.sentence: From a small comic publisher in 1939 to the architect of a cinematic multiverse, I turned humble beginnings into an enduring legacy through risk, sacrifice, and the timeless power of great power and responsibility.
levels.paragraph: I began as Timely Comics, a small publisher with a wild hope, and I learned that a single issue could spark an entire universe. I became a wartime hero, faded into quiet, then rose again in the 1960s with flawed, human heroes who argued and struggled like real people. Over the decades, I faced heartbreaking decisions and financial collapse, but cinema gave me new life and let me tell stories on a cosmic scale. Today, after Thanos and Endgame, I feel both pride and sorrow, yet I'm ready for whatever comes next.
levels.summary:
I started as Timely Comics in 1939, and the surprising success of Marvel Comics #1 planted the seeds of a universe. I became Captain America in 1941, a symbol of hope and wartime fury, but faded after the war.

In the 1960s I remade myself as Marvel, launching the Fantastic Four with real problems and arguing heroes, then Spider-Man, whose 'great responsibility' ethic became my guiding thread. I introduced the X-Men and Avengers, and quietly debuted T'Challa as the Black Panther, never making a fuss—he was simply great.

Later decades brought darker turns: I killed Gwen Stacy, corrupted Jean Grey into the Dark Phoenix, and saw Captain America assassinated after Civil War. I filed for bankruptcy in 1996, only to be resurrected by cinema—X-Men in 2000, Iron Man in 2008, and the Infinity Saga culminating in 2019's Endgame.

Through sacrifice and loss, I learned that heroes are defined by consequences, and that conviction matters more than immediate success. Watching half of Earth's heroes turn to dust, then seeing Tony Stark sacrifice everything, left me proud, heartbroken, and ready to move forward.
